# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Clinical and Technical Overview

Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has revolutionized the treatment of severe symptomatic aortic stenosis. While transfemoral access remains the gold standard, a substantial subset of patients presents with hostile, severely diseased, tortuous, or calcified iliofemoral arteries that preclude the safe delivery of large-bore sheaths [1, 2]. Traditionally, surgical alternative access routes, such as transapical, transaortic, and transsubclavian/axillary access, were utilized to bypass these anatomical limitations [3, 4]. However, these surgical approaches are associated with increased morbidity, longer recovery times, and higher rates of major complications [5, 6]. Transcaval (cavoaortic) access has emerged as a completely percutaneous, highly effective alternative to surgical cutdown, enabling large-bore structural heart interventions through the retroperitoneal venous system [7, 8].

### Technical Principles and Procedural Planning

Transcaval access involves crossing from the inferior vena cava (IVC) into the adjacent abdominal aorta, tracking a guidewire, and placing a large-bore sheath [9]. Contrast-enhanced multidetector computed tomography (MDCT) is essential for pre-procedural planning [10]. MDCT allows clinicians to evaluate the spatial relationship between the IVC and abdominal aorta, identify a calcium-free target zone on the aortic wall, and ensure the absence of intervening retroperitoneal structures, such as bowel loops or major branch vessels [11, 12].

Procedurally, access is obtained via the femoral vein and femoral artery [13]. A catheter is positioned in the abdominal aorta as a target, while a crossing system is advanced into the IVC [14]. Electrosurgical crossing is performed by delivering radiofrequency energy through a dedicated guidewire, allowing it to vaporize tissue and cross the cavoaortic space into the target aortic lumen under fluoroscopic guidance [15, 16]. Once the wire is secured in the aorta, the channel is dilated, and a large-bore sheath is introduced into the aorta to facilitate the structural intervention, such as TAVR [17].

Following the primary procedure, the transcaval tract is closed percutaneously using an off-label nitinol cardiac septal occluder, typically an Amplatzer Duct Occluder (ADO) [18, 19]. The self-expanding nitinol device is deployed across the aortocaval tract, plugging the hole. Persistent, low-pressure aortocaval shunting immediately after deployment is common but typically resolves spontaneously or via tissue tract thrombosis, while retroperitoneal hemorrhage is prevented by the surrounding retroperitoneal pressure gradient [20, 21].

### Clinical Evidence and Safety Profile

The clinical utility of transcaval access was first validated in human trials by Greenbaum and colleagues [1]. The prospective, multicenter National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) transcaval registry demonstrated a high rate of successful transcaval crossing and deployment (99%), with low 30-day mortality and stroke rates, especially considering the high-risk patient cohort [2].

Comparative studies have consistently shown that transcaval access is superior to surgical alternative access methods. For instance, propensity-matched cohort studies comparing transcaval to transapical and transaortic access demonstrated shorter hospital stays, less post-procedural pain, and lower rates of acute kidney injury and bleeding complications in patients undergoing transcaval TAVR [22-24]. Furthermore, when compared directly with transaxillary access, transcaval access shows comparable safety and efficacy, positioning it as a first-line alternative when transfemoral access is unfeasible [25, 26].

### Expanded Indications and Future Directions

While TAVR remains the primary indication, the utility of transcaval access has expanded to other large-bore interventions [27]. It has been successfully used to deliver thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) and endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) grafts in patients with severely diseased iliofemoral anatomy [28]. Additionally, transcaval access has been utilized for the insertion of temporary mechanical circulatory support (MCS) devices, such as the Impella 5.0 or 5.5, facilitating hemodynamic support in patients undergoing high-risk percutaneous coronary intervention or cardiogenic shock management [29].

Despite its clinical success, challenges remain, including the off-label use of cardiac septal occluders for closure and the potential for rare but serious complications such as retroperitoneal bleeding, aortic dissection, or persistent symptomatic aortocaval fistulas [30]. The development of dedicated, purpose-built transcaval closure devices and standardized training programs will be crucial to further improve safety profiles and integrate this technique into the routine armamentarium of structural heart teams globally.

### Conclusion

Transcaval access represents a major milestone in percutaneous cardiovascular medicine. By converting an arterial procedure into a venous-based access strategy, it offers a safe, reliable, and less invasive pathway for patients requiring large-bore structural heart and aortic interventions who lack conventional transfemoral options.
